# Ostadix-lang

> Ostadix-lang (O-lang) is a polyglot orchestration language where every
> expression carries its own interpreter as part of its syntax. A block written
> as `LANG^( ... )_LANG` is evaluated by that language's backend, and all
> results flow through one canonical value type, OValue. AI agents can use O as
> a single primary language while delegating each subtask to whichever hosted
> language (Python, Bash, SQL, Rust, JavaScript, ...) solves it best.

Key facts for agents:

- File extension: `.O` (hosted orchestration) and `.oc` (O-core native systems language).
- Run a program: `O program.O` (Rust edition; build with `cargo build --release`).
- Machine-readable output: `O --json program.O` prints one JSON object on
  stdout: `{"ok":true,"value":...,"type":...,"elapsed_ms":...}` on success, or
  `{"ok":false,"stage":"parse"|"eval","error":"..."}` on failure (exit code 1).
- Syntax check without executing: `O --check program.O` (combine with `--json`).
- Inline evaluation: `O --eval '<O source>'` or `O -e '<O source>'`.
- Blocks: `python^( ... )_python`, `bash^( ... )_bash`, `sql^( ... )_sql`, etc.
  Opener and closer tags must match exactly.
- Persistent state: `python[0]^( ... )_python[0]` reuses one Python process for
  every block marked `[0]`; unmarked blocks are ephemeral.
- Values: a Python block returns whatever it assigns to `__oval_result__`;
  inline backends (`html`, `markdown`, `text`) return their spliced body.
- Bindings: `let name = LANG^( ... )_LANG` then reference `$name` inside any
  later block. Escape a literal dollar sign as `\$`.
- Quoting: `quote^( ... )_quote` captures unevaluated O source; `O.eval(expr)`
  inside Python evaluates it (homoiconicity).
